name: kaitai-struct-compiler
desc: Compiler for generating binary data parsers
why: Describe a binary format in YAML and generate parsers for it, a strong tool for taking file formats apart.

brief.what_it_is: Kaitai Struct is a declarative language for describing binary data layouts, such as file formats and network packet formats, in a .ksy file. The ksc compiler takes that .ksy file and generates source code for a parser in one of the supported programming languages. The generated code reads the described structure from a file or stream and exposes its fields through an API. The site lists C++/STL, C#, Go, Java, JavaScript, Lua, Nim, Perl, PHP, Python, Ruby, and Rust as targets, with Swift listed among runtime libraries. The project also ships an IDE, a visualizer, and a library of format descriptions.
brief.why_it_exists: The homepage says that reading and writing binary formats is hard, especially for interchange formats that must work across platforms and languages, and that hand-written parsing code is repetitive, error-prone, and hard to debug. The goal is to describe the format once and use it from any supported language.
brief.how_it_works: You write a .ksy file that declares the format, using fields such as seq with types like u2 and u4, plus endianness and nested types. You can check the parse with the visualizer, then compile the .ksy with ksc into a source file for your target language. You add the small KS runtime library for that language to your project, and the generated class parses the data and gives access to its fields.

commands_seen.context: Homebrew install of the compiler on macOS or Linux, listed as the Homebrew option under Downloading and installing.
Downloads the stable 0.11 .deb package for Debian or Ubuntu.
Installs the downloaded .deb package on a Debian-based Linux system.
Clones the umbrella repository with all sub-projects as submodules, for building from source.
Fixes a clone that was made without --recurse-submodules.

brief.install_notes: Homebrew is the simplest route on macOS or Linux, and the homepage lists no extra requirements for it. The .deb route is for Debian-based Linux. Windows users get an MSI installer, or a portable universal .zip. The .zip and MSI need Java, with LTS 21 recommended and Java 8 as the minimum, and the universal build bundles its jars and launcher scripts. Building from source needs git, Java, sbt, and a POSIX shell for tests. Your project also needs the KS runtime library for its language. The runtimes are described as small.
brief.standout: One declarative description can generate parsers for more than a dozen languages, so the .ksy file becomes a shared, language-neutral spec of the format. The ecosystem around it (visualizer, IDE, and a public gallery of format descriptions) is unusually complete for a parser generator.
brief.status: Appears maintained. The homepage shows version 0.11 released 2025-09-07 and links stable downloads to that release. I did not check the GitHub commit history, so activity beyond that release date is unconfirmed.
brief.caveats: The homepage notes that development (unstable) builds that were once on Bintray are not currently available. Distribution moved to GitHub Releases in 2021, and the page mentions a planned replacement repository that is not yet live. The compiler and visualizer are GPLv3+, while the runtime libraries are MIT, Apache v2 (JavaScript), or MIT for the rest. The non-Homebrew builds require Java. The 'Built with Kaitai Struct' list names projects such as mitmproxy and OWASP ZAP. I only read the homepage, so the format gallery and the documentation were not checked.
quotes: Describe the format once and then everybody can use it from their programming languages — cross-language, cross-platform.
Declarative: describe the very structure of the data, not how you read or write it
Packed with tools and samples: includes a compiler, an IDE, a visualizer and massive library of popular formats
